questions.question:
D7 — Who is allowed to write to the cache adapter?
Project/branch/task: main branch, /plan-eng-review of PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor" (Architecture review).
ELI10: Two services both write into the same cache (PLAN.md:29), and the adapter's own rules say writes are not serialized (PLAN.md:19). Picture SessionMint waiting on the identity provider while, in that gap, the tenant gets suspended and the invalidation hook wipes their entries. The mint finishes and writes a fresh entry for a tenant who should now be locked out. Two writers make that race easy; one writer that re-checks tenant status right before storing makes it hard.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A suspended or logged-out tenant keeps a live cached session until expiry, which is exactly the class of bug the invalidation hooks exist to prevent.
Recommendation: A because a single writer is the simplest explicit structure, needs no change to the adapter or its tests, and puts the one write site next to the one policy check in AuthBroker.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, D=3/10; C is an investigation step, unscored
Pros / cons:
A) Single writer: only AuthBroker writes (recommended)
  ✅ One write site to audit; SessionMint becomes side-effect free and trivially testable
  ✅ Adapter and its existing tests stay unchanged; broker re-checks tenant status before the write
  ❌ SessionMint must return the minted session instead of storing it, a small API change (human: ~3h / CC: ~10 min)
B) Both write, through one guarded adapter write path
  ✅ Closes the race for every present and future writer at the adapter boundary
  ✅ Services keep their proposed write calls
  ❌ Changes the adapter contract the plan promised to leave unchanged (PLAN.md:21-22); its tests must grow (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
C) Investigate before choosing
  ✅ A bounded read of the adapter's hooks and mint write sites confirms or dismisses the race
  ✅ No structural commitment on an inferred risk
  ❌ Leaves a P1 open into implementation; the probe still ends in this same choice
D) Both services write directly, as planned
  ✅ No API change to SessionMint or the adapter
  ✅ Matches the plan as written
  ❌ Leaves the mint-after-invalidate race open with no mitigation
Net: one write site with a tenant re-check vs. two writers racing the invalidation hooks.

questions.question:
D8 — What happens when validateAndDispatch() hits an error?
Project/branch/task: main branch, /plan-eng-review of PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor" (Architecture review, security).
ELI10: The function that decides whether a request gets through has three nested try/catch blocks, and each one catches an error and moves on (PLAN.md:32-33). In an auth path, "catch and move on" is the dangerous direction: if a token check throws and the code keeps going, a bad token might be dispatched as if it were fine. The safe rule is fail closed: any error while validating or checking policy means deny, with a typed error that says which stage failed, and nothing is dispatched.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Fail open means an IDP hiccup or a malformed token could let a request through with no log line to find it later; fail closed means an IDP outage denies logins loudly, which is the outcome you want.
Recommendation: A because auth must fail closed, typed errors make the three failure stages testable and greppable, and letting dispatch errors propagate keeps the broker from hiding downstream bugs.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Pros / cons:
A) Fail closed: validate/policy errors deny with typed errors; dispatch errors propagate (recommended)
  ✅ No path from a swallowed error to a dispatched request; each stage has a named error class to assert on
  ✅ Every denial is logged with tenant and request id, so a 3am incident has a trail
  ❌ An IDP or cache outage becomes visible login failures rather than silent degradation (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
B) Fail closed for validate and policy; keep swallowing dispatch errors
  ✅ Closes the security-relevant fail-open path
  ✅ Smaller change to the dispatch stage as written
  ❌ Downstream dispatch bugs stay invisible; callers cannot distinguish "dispatched" from "failed silently"
C) Keep the three swallowing catches as planned
  ✅ No change to the proposed function
  ✅ Zero risk of newly visible failures
  ❌ Unknown fail-open behavior in the auth decision path, untestable by error class
Net: loud, typed denials vs. silent continues in the one function that must never be silent.
